To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
muscarinic acetylc choline receptors (M3) inhibit an outward potassium current in cerebellar granular neurons (CGNs).

muscarine inhibits a K+ channel in CGNs by acting on M3 muscari nic acetylcholine (mACh) receptors and that this inhibition is not dependent on Ca2+ mobilization from intracellular stores.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of intracellular Ca2+ stores and the two‐pores domain K+ channels in the regulation of neuronal excitability.
the role of intracellular Ca2+ in the regulation of potassium channels and in particular with the effects of muscarinic receptors on potassium channels.
the role of Ca2+-dependent and Ca2+-independent mechanisms in the regulation of the K+ channel TASK-1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
muscarinic inhibition and muscarinic Ca2+ release are two separate and distinct actions of the M3 receptor in these neurons.
the inhibition of IK(S0) by M3 receptors is a direct effect of the receptor, and not a consequence of the mobilization of intracellular Ca2+.
muscarinic inhibition is not mediated via the mobilization of intracellular calcium stores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
muscarinic inhibition is not mediated by a rise in [Ca2+].
the M3 receptor‐mediated inhibition of IK(SA) in CGNs is not due to the activation of PLC or the release of Ca2+ from internal stores.
muscarine inhibits IK(SO) by a mechanism that is independent of Ca2+ release from intracellular Ca2+ stores.
The main takeaway from our work is that
muscarinic acetycholine receptors can act as ion channels in the absence of G‐protein coupling.
the inhibition of IK(So) in CGNs is mediated through a direct action of muscarinic agonists at the M3 receptor and that the mobilization of intracellular Ca2+ is not a prerequisite for this action.

the inhibition of IK(So) by muscarine in neonatal rat granule cells is not due to the mobilization of intracellular Ca2+, but instead is likely to be due to direct activation of the M3 muscarine receptor.
